research_question: Hvordan er forestillinger om verk, originalitet og komponistautoritet blitt historisk produsert?

bibliographic_identity.title: Musical Samplers in the Museum of Musical Works: The Nature, Status, and Value of Nineteenth-Century Oxford Degree Exercises
bibliographic_identity.publication: Journal of the Royal Musical Association 150(1), 187–222

production_source_extensions.registration_reason: Open-access, peer-reviewed study of identified Oxford degree-exercise manuscripts. The article documents the institutional purpose and conventions of the exercise corpus, gives object-level analysis and shelfmark control for William Crotch's 1794 BMus exercise, and separates academic, archival, performing and musicological value when discussing work status and canon.

locators.section: Institutional identity and purpose of the musical exercise
locators.supports: Golding identifies the British musical exercise as composition produced for university accreditation, documents its own rituals, conventions and codes of practice, and explains that the archive exposes what the academic establishment valued and expected composers to demonstrate.

locators.section: William Crotch, O Sing unto the Lord, Bodleian MS. Mus. Sch. Ex. d37
locators.supports: The object is identified as Crotch's 1794 BMus exercise. Golding documents its voices, orchestra, multi-movement structure and genre ambiguity: it is described as an anthem but analysed as closer to a cantata. The score is manuscript, annotated and corrected; the programme is printed; no publication or later performance is documented.

locators.section: Musical Exercises and Problems of Value in Music History; Conclusion
locators.supports: Golding shows that the exercises were created as demonstrations of academic skills, mostly outside normal public-performance circulation, and distinguishes their value as historical objects from admission to a performing canon. The conclusion explicitly separates performing and musicological canons and rejects a history limited to long-lived, publicly successful works.

source_reviews.rights_and_reuse_note: The article is publisher-hosted open access under CC BY 4.0. History Go stores bibliographic identity, locators and paraphrased findings. The Bodleian manuscript remains an external catalog object; no manuscript image or score is redistributed.

claim_records.statement: William Crotchs O Sing unto the Lord fra 1794 kan ikke forstås uttømmende gjennom én tidløs verkstatus. Det identifiserte manuskriptet ble produsert og vurdert som en Oxford-gradskomposisjon: en institusjonell demonstrasjon av bestemte ferdigheter og konvensjoner. Samtidig har det en navngitt komponist, sammenhengende musikalsk struktur, varig arkividentitet og senere analytisk lesbarhet. Goldings fulltekststudie viser at gradskomposisjonene stort sett sirkulerte utenfor offentlig konsert- og publiseringsliv, og skiller deres historiske og musikkvitenskapelige verdi fra opptak i framføringskanonen. I dette avgrensede caset blir derfor 'verk' og 'kanon' institusjonelt produserte klassifikasjoner: eksamen, arkiv, analyse og framføring autoriserer ulike sider av samme objekt, uten at fravær fra framføringskanonen dokumenterer lav estetisk kvalitet.

claim_records.uncertainty: The selected direct object is one Oxford exercise within Golding's broader British and Oxford corpus. The official catalog and article agree on identity and attribution, but History Go has not independently inspected the full manuscript or reconstructed its examination performance. No publication or later performance was found in the reviewed study; this is bounded negative evidence, not proof that no undocumented use ever occurred.
claim_records.prohibited_inference: Do not infer that the object is not music, that it lacks aesthetic value, that every degree exercise has the same status, that university accreditation makes it canonical, that archival preservation proves public influence, that absence from the performing canon demonstrates deliberate exclusion, or that the modern autonomous-work concept was the actors' only operative category in 1794.

boundary_records.statement: Crotch-manuskriptet og Goldings Oxford-korpus dokumenterer én historisk institusjonell form for gradskomposisjon; caset kan ikke definere verkstatus, forfatterskap eller kanon for alle tider, steder, sjangre og praksiser.
boundary_records.release_effect: Keeps the claim object- and institution-bounded and blocks universal work-ontology language.

boundary_records.statement: Manglende dokumentasjon av publisering eller senere framføring av O Sing unto the Lord kan brukes til å avgrense sirkulasjonen, men kan ikke alene bevise lav estetisk kvalitet, uviktighet eller bevisst eksklusjon.
boundary_records.release_effect: Separates documented circulation history from aesthetic judgment and causal exclusion claims.

boundary_records.statement: At Bodleian-katalogen og den gjennomgåtte studien attribuerer manuskriptet til Crotch løser objektidentiteten for dette caset, men komponistnavnet avgjør ikke alene om objektet skal klassifiseres som øvelse, verk, artefakt eller kanonisk repertoar.
boundary_records.release_effect: Allows stable attribution while blocking composer-name substitution for work- and canon-history.

boundary_records.statement: Arkivbevaring, katalogisering og musikkvitenskapelig analyse gjør objektet inspectable og historisk relevant, men etablerer ikke i seg selv opptak i en framføringskanon eller dokumentert offentlig resepsjon.
boundary_records.release_effect: Separates archival and musicological authorization from performance circulation and reception.

resolved: The Bodleian catalog provides a persistent institutional record, title, attributed composer and shelfmark for MS. Mus. Sch. Ex. d. 37.
Golding 2025 provides publisher-hosted open full text under CC BY 4.0 and identifies the same object as Crotch's 1794 Oxford BMus exercise.
Table 1, Figure 1 and pp. 196–198 provide multiple object-level locators for structure, scoring, genre, manuscript state and circulation history.
The institutional purpose is documented as university accreditation and skill demonstration rather than inferred from musical style alone.
The article's ontology and conclusion sections distinguish archival/musicological value from performing-canon status.
Inference boundaries block aesthetic ranking, universal work ontology, attribution overreach, deliberate-exclusion claims and archive-to-performance substitution.
The manuscript object remains external_link_and_metadata_only; no score or image is redistributed.
direct_object_gate.release_rule: Only the bounded claim that Oxford examination, archival preservation, musicological analysis and performance circulation authorize different statuses of this identified object may drive questions. Preserve the negative-evidence and aesthetic-judgment boundaries.

coverage.known_gap: This production does not establish a universal theory of musical works, independently analyse the manuscript, reconstruct the 1794 examination performance, document every later use, or explain canon formation across other repertoires. It opens one institutionally and materially bounded Oxford case.
